title: The Negative Superpower
subtitle: Negative Fundamentals · Mission 05
tagline: Today you {{amber:switch sides}}. The Negative team doesn't build — they {{amber:break}}. Learn the two attack routes and the six-step formula that dismantles any plan.

slides.headline: 🛡️ SWITCH SIDES, DEBATER
body: You know that one friend who *always* plays devil's advocate? 😏 The one who hears any idea and says **"Actually, that's not true because..."**?
In policy debate, that friend has a name: the {{amber: Negative}}. And being negative isn't rude — it's a {{amber: superpower}}.
The Aff has to build a whole plan. You don't. Your only job is to prove their plan is a {{amber: bad idea}}. You poke holes. You ask hard questions. You stop a weak plan before it gets a vote. 🎯
Today: meet your two attack routes and the six-step formula that turns any hole into a knockout. 💥

items.label: Define the {{amber: Negative}}'s job in a policy round
Tell apart {{cyan: on-case}} and {{amber: off-case}} attacks
Run the {{amber: ITAPIN}} formula to dismantle an argument

slides.definition: The {{amber: Negative}} is the team that says *NO* to the resolution. Their job is to prove the {{cyan: Affirmative}}'s plan is a **bad idea** — either because it won't work, or because it makes something else worse. 🛡️
slides.plainWords: You're the defense. You don't have to fix anything. You just have to show what's broken with their fix.
slides.analogy: Think of it like a {{amber: shield}}. The Aff throws a plan at the judge. You block it, break it, or turn it around. If nothing gets through, you win. 🛡️

slides.headline: TWO WAYS TO ATTACK
slides.intro: The Negative team gets two attack routes. You can hit the Aff's plan head-on, or bring in a totally new reason it's a bad idea. Some rounds you'll use one. Great debaters use both.

cards.name: ON-CASE
cards.description: Attack the plan {{cyan: head-on}}. Say the problem isn't big. Say nobody's really hurt. Say it's already being fixed. Or say the plan won't {{cyan: actually work}}.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "Their plan won't fix hunger. Free lunch programs already fail in most schools."

cards.name: OFF-CASE
cards.description: Bring a {{amber: new}} reason the plan is bad. Even if it works, it causes a whole new problem the Aff didn't warn the judge about.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "Sure, the plan might help schools. But it costs so much it crashes the economy."

cards.name: THE NEG BLOCK
cards.description: The {{amber: Neg}}'s secret weapon: **13 straight minutes** of back-to-back speeches (2NC + 1NR) that the Aff can't interrupt. Use it to bury them in attacks.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "That's five arguments the 1AR has to answer in five minutes. Good luck."

slides.headline: ⚡ THE ITAPIN FORMULA
slides.intro: Knowing when to attack isn't enough. You need to know *how*. Every time you refute an argument, run the six-step {{amber: ITAPIN}} sequence — in order. The word spells the first letter of each step.

rows.name: 🎯 I — Identify
rows.description: Name the exact argument you're attacking. Not "their whole case." One argument. Point to it so the judge knows where to look.

rows.name: 🗣️ T — They Say
rows.description: Repeat what the Aff claimed in their own words. This shows the judge you were {{cyan: listening}} — and it locks in what you're about to break.

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"They say their plan reduces poverty by 50%."*

rows.name: 🥊 A — Argument
rows.description: Tell the judge {{amber: why they're wrong}}. This is your counter-attack. One clear sentence beats a paragraph of mush.

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"We say that number is way too high — it's not realistic."*

rows.name: 🏆 P — Prefer because
rows.description: Explain why the judge should believe {{amber: you}} over them. Your logic, your evidence, your source — what makes your side stronger?

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"Prefer our argument because a similar plan in the past only cut poverty by 2%."*

rows.name: 💥 I — Impact
rows.description: Say {{amber: why it matters}} for the round. Not just "they're wrong" — but *"because they're wrong, you can't vote for their plan."*

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"Because their plan doesn't solve, you cannot vote Aff."*

rows.name: 📄 N — New Evidence
rows.description: Back it up with a fresh {{cyan: card}}. New quote, new source, new proof. Optional — but a card sells the point to the judge.

prompt.label: QUICK CHECK
prompt.question: 🛡️ What is the {{amber: Negative}} team's job in a policy round?

options.text: Bring their own plan and prove it works
Prove the Affirmative's plan is a bad idea
Agree with the Affirmative and add more evidence

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: Locked in. The {{amber: Neg}} doesn't have to build anything — they just have to **break** the Aff's plan. Poke holes. Show what's wrong. Stop the plan before it gets a vote.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** This is why the Neg is a *superpower*. The Aff has to defend a whole plan. You only have to find **one** thing wrong with it.

a.title: ✕ WRONG TEAM
body: The {{cyan: Aff}} brings a plan. The {{amber: Neg}} tears one down. You don't need your own plan — you just need to prove theirs is a **bad idea**.

c.title: ✕ OPPOSITE JOB
body: The Neg *disagrees* with the Aff. If you agreed, there'd be no debate. Your job is to show the plan is {{amber: broken}}.

d.title: ✕ THAT'S THE JUDGE
body: The {{cyan: Judge}} picks the winner. The {{amber: Neg}}'s job is to **argue** — specifically, to argue the Aff's plan is a bad idea.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: B}}. The Neg's whole job is proving the Aff's plan is a **bad idea**.

prompt.label: ATTACK ROUTE MATCH
prompt.scenario: Match each Negative attack to the right route.
prompt.question: Drag each attack on the left to {{cyan: ON-CASE}} or {{amber: OFF-CASE}} on the right.

items.text: "Nobody is really being hurt right now."
⚡ OFF-CASE — brings a NEW reason the plan is bad

correct.title: ✓ ROUTES LOCKED IN
body: Clean match. {{cyan: On-case}} attacks live *inside* the Aff's plan — the problem, the harms, the solvency. {{amber: Off-case}} attacks come from *outside* — new consequences the Aff didn't see coming.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** The strongest Neg strategies run *both* routes. Break their case AND show a new problem. Now the Aff has to defend on two fronts.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ ROUTES CROSSED
body: Quick test: is the attack {{cyan: about the plan itself}} (won't work, problem isn't big, nobody hurt)? → **On-case**. Or does it bring a {{amber: new bad thing}} the plan causes? → **Off-case**.

prompt.label: STOCK ISSUE READ
prompt.scenario:
The Affirmative just said: *"Our plan will fix hunger because schools will give every kid free lunch."* 🍎

You stand up and say: *"Their plan won't actually work — free lunch programs already fail in most schools."*
prompt.question: Which {{cyan: on-case}} stock issue are you attacking?

options.text: Significance — you're saying the problem isn't big enough
Harms — you're saying nobody is really hurt
Inherency — you're saying it's already being fixed
Solvency — you're saying their plan won't actually work

correct.title: ✓ CLEAN HIT
body: Right. When you say *"their plan won't work,"* you're attacking {{amber: Solvency}} — the stock issue that asks: *does the plan actually fix the problem?* 🎯
correct.followup: **Memory trick:** Every on-case attack lines up with one of the {{cyan: 4 stock issues}}: **Significance** (size), **Harms** (hurt), **Inherency** (already fixed), or **Solvency** (does it work).

a.title: ✕ WRONG STOCK ISSUE
body: {{cyan: Significance}} asks *"is the problem big enough to care about?"* You weren't attacking how big hunger is. You were attacking the **plan itself** — that's {{amber: Solvency}}.

b.title: ✕ WRONG STOCK ISSUE
body: {{cyan: Harms}} asks *"is anyone really getting hurt?"* You weren't saying kids aren't hungry. You were saying the plan {{amber: won't work}} — that's Solvency.

c.title: ✕ WRONG STOCK ISSUE
body: {{cyan: Inherency}} asks *"is someone already fixing this?"* You didn't say free lunch is already happening. You said {{amber: their fix doesn't fix it}} — that's Solvency.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: D — Solvency}}. Re-read what you said: *"Their plan won't actually work."* That sentence attacks the plan itself.

prompt.label: BUILD THE ATTACK
prompt.scenario: Your Neg partner started an {{amber: ITAPIN}} attack — but the lines are scrambled. Sort each line into either the {{cyan: SETUP}} half (Identify + They Say + Argument) or the {{amber: FINISH}} half (Prefer + Impact + New Evidence).
prompt.question: Drop each line into the right half.

cards.text: "They say their plan cuts poverty by 50%." 🗣️
"We say that number is way too high." 🥊
"Prefer our argument — a real plan only cut it by 2%." 🏆
"Because their plan doesn't solve, you can't vote Aff." 💥

correct.title: ✓ FORMULA ASSEMBLED
body: Clean sort. The {{cyan: setup}} names the target, repeats what they said, and lands your point. The {{amber: finish}} tells the judge *why to prefer you*, *why it matters*, and *what proof you've got*.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Weak Negs stop after the Argument step. Great Negs {{amber: always}} do the finish — that's what actually wins the argument on the flow.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISALIGNED
body: Litmus test: if the line is telling the judge *what you're attacking or why they're wrong*, it's {{cyan: setup}}. If it's telling the judge *why to prefer you, why it matters, or handing them proof*, it's {{amber: finish}}.

prompt.label: FIELD DEPLOYMENT
prompt.scenario: The Affirmative just said: *"Our plan reduces poverty by 50%."* You're on your feet. Fill in your ITAPIN attack.
prompt.question: Drop the right word into each blank.

slides.template:
Identify: Look at their {{1}} argument.

They Say: They say their plan cuts poverty by 50%.

Argument: We say that number is way too {{2}}.

Prefer because: A similar plan in the past only cut poverty by {{3}}%.

blanks.hint: Which stock issue asks 'does the plan actually work?'
50% is unrealistic — the number is too ___
From the briefing — a real plan only cut it by this much.

correct.title: ✓ FORMULA DEPLOYED
body: That's a real ITAPIN attack. You named the target ({{amber: Solvency}}), repeated what they claimed, said why they're wrong (number too high), and backed it up with proof (only 2% in real life).
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Add the {{amber: Impact}} step — *"because their plan doesn't solve, you can't vote Aff"* — and the {{amber: New Evidence}} step, and you've got a full refutation the judge can flow.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REBUILD
body: Three checkpoints: {{cyan: Solvency}} = the stock issue about whether the plan works. If 50% is unrealistic, the number is too {{cyan: high}}. And the example proof said a real plan only cut poverty by {{cyan: 2}}%.

prompt.label: BIG IDEA CHECK
prompt.question: 🎯 What makes the {{amber: Negative}} different from just being *that friend who disagrees with everything*?

options.text: The Neg follows a formula (ITAPIN) and attacks with evidence — not just gut reactions
The Neg only disagrees about food and phones
There's no difference — both are just being negative

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE GAME
body: Exactly. A contrarian friend just says *"nuh-uh."* A {{amber: Neg debater}} names the argument, repeats it, breaks it, tells you why to prefer their side, why it matters, and reads a card. That's not being negative — that's being {{amber: precise}}. 🎯
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** This is why {{amber: Neg}} is a superpower and not a personality trait. Anyone can disagree. Only a debater can *refute*.

b.title: ✕ LOUDER ISN'T BETTER
body: Yelling loses rounds in debate. The Neg wins with {{amber: structure}} — the ITAPIN formula — not volume.

c.title: ✕ NOT THE TOPIC
body: The Neg can argue against {{amber: anything}} the Aff proposes — plans, harms, evidence, solutions. The difference isn't *what* they argue. It's {{amber: how}}.

d.title: ✕ THERE'S A BIG DIFFERENCE
body: A contrarian friend disagrees with a shrug. A {{amber: Neg}} disagrees with a **6-step formula**, evidence, and a plan to change the judge's mind. That's the game.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: A}}. What separates a Neg from a contrarian is {{amber: ITAPIN}} plus evidence — structure, not attitude.

slides.headline: BRIEFING COMPLETE ✅
slides.subtext: You've got the Negative Superpower. Two attack routes: {{cyan: on-case}} (hit the plan) and {{amber: off-case}} (bring a new problem). One formula: {{amber: ITAPIN}} — Identify, They Say, Argument, Prefer, Impact, New Evidence. The bridge opens up. 🛡️
